title: Kate and Rooney Mara Talk ‘Bucking Fastard,’ Synchronized Sisterhood and Werner Herzog Life Lessons: “He Doesn’t Give a S***”
full_text: × Skip to main content Rooney Mara, Werner Herzog and Kate Mara attend the 'Bucking Fastard' world premiere during the 83rd Venice Film Festival at Sala Grande on September 3, 2026. (Photo by Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images) Werner Herzog has a bit of a wild reputation . He’d like to set the record straight. “I’m the most organized, the most focused, the most friendly person you will ever see on a set,” the German director says. “Period.” Everything else, he adds, is “the craze of media who want to create a Werner Herzog that is a fiction.” This is, of course, the man who hauled a 320-ton steamship over a hill in the Peruvian jungle for Fitzcarraldo (1982), and, on the shoot of Aguirre, the Wrath of God (1972), also in the jungle, threatened to kill his star Klaus Kinski if he walked away from the film [as recounted by Herzog himself in his 1999 documentary My Best Fiend .] This is the man who ate his own shoe after losing a bet to Errol Morris, and who once carried on with a BBC interview after being hit by an air rifle, calling it “not a significant bullet.” Related Stories Movies Paul Schrader Tears Up at 'The Basics of Philosophy' Venice Premiere Movies 'The Basics of Philosophy' Review: Paul Schrader Does Some Deep -- and Discomfiting -- Thinking About a College Professor's Guilt But when Herzog came calling, Kate and Rooney Mara signed up anyway. The Mara sisters play the leads in Herzog’s Bucking Fastard , as Jean and Joan Holbrooke, Irish sisters who speak, think and move in unison, share the same dreams and love the same man. After their neighbor and former lover Gareth Mulroney (Orlando Bloom) marries someone else, the sisters embark on a campaign of arson, ambush and assorted misdemeanors to win him back, become tabloid fixtures and are assigned a social worker (Domhnall Gleeson) to help them adapt to modern life. They eventually decamp to Ireland’s West Coast to live with their widowed aunt (Marion O’Dwyer), where they begin chipping away at a cave in a mountain range, convinced the tunnel will lead them to the Orkney Islands, in their minds a mythical place where true love is possible. The film is loosely inspired by Freda and Greta Chaplin, identical twins from York, in northern England, who spoke in unison and became widely known after a 1981 court case made them tabloid sensations. HanWay Films is handling worldwide sales. Bucking Fastard premiered in competition at the Venice Film Festival Thursday night , drawing a warm six-and-a-half-minute standing ovation for Herzog and his cast. Sitting down with THR ahead of the premiere, Herzog and the Maras spoke about their synchronized performance, the film’s surprising vein of “Bavarian humor” and Herzog life lessons in “really not giving a shit.” Why did you both want to work with Werner Herzog? ROONEY MARA For every reason under the sun. I would have loved to have just been a PA on the set, just to watch him in action. It’s one of the greatest experiences one can have. KATE MARA I’ve been fascinated by the way Werner makes films ever since I saw one of his documentaries, so to get to work on a film with him has always been a dream. And then to read his script about these sisters and their bond and this love story was incredibly magical. There are a lot of stories about the extremes you have gone to on films. Did you have any trepidation? KATE MARA Zero trepidation about that. The scariest thing for us was just: How are we going to do this? How are we going to do an entire film in unison and in sync in that way? But I had zero worries about working with Werner. WERNER HERZOG I can tell you why: because I’m the most organized, the most focused, the most friendly person you will ever see on a set. Period. Everything you’re hinting at is the craze of media who want to create a Werner Herzog that is a fiction. KATE MARA It’s passion. To me, that’s one of the most important things you need in a director — passion, and somebody who cares deeply about filmmaking. Why did you want the two Mara sisters for this dual role? HERZOG I had a story, and I thought about whether it should be twins. And I found the two sisters, and it was immediately clear this was finally a solution. I wrote the screenplay very quickly, in five days, and we were done with pre-production in five, six weeks and started to film. We had some rehearsal time, the first time in my life, in all of my films, that there was enough money to do rehearsals. We had two weeks. After a week, I said, “Stop this. Meet me in front of my camera. You’re so good. Stop it.” ‘Bucking Fastard’ with Rooney Mara, Kate Mara Courtesy of Lena Herzog Speaking and moving simultaneously is central to the performances. How did you find a way to do that as actors? KATE MARA It felt very much like a song, like a rhythm. Once we figured out what that song was and what the rhythm was — which happened way faster than we thought it would — it just made sense to us. It was an unspoken sort of thing. Rooney and I worked a lot together before working with Werner, trying to find our tricks. ROONEY MARA We had a voice coach we worked with before Werner, who gave us tips, exercises we did together. We weren’t really sure until we got into rehearsal with Werner. We were like, “What the hell are we doing? What is this?” And then when we started doing it in front of him, he liked it so much. It flowed more naturally than we had anticipated. HERZOG By the way, we did very few takes. I would shoot two or three takes, and that was normally it. Sometimes a single take for a very long scene. Period. I’m a one-camera guy. I do hardly any coverage. There was no coverage. Two shots, and that was it. Two takes. KATE MARA We would be done hours early sometimes. HERZOG We finished at 3 p.m., 3:30 in the afternoon. We could have gone until 5, 6, 7 without overtime, and I said, “Let’s wrap it.” I’m not exaggerating, and the film was done under schedule and under budget. You’ve compared this film thematically to Fitzcarraldo and Grizzly Man . Where do you see the connection? HERZOG We shouldn’t overdo the connections. But with Fitzcarraldo , it is evident: There is a great dream about opera in the jungle, and for that the protagonist moves a big ship over a mountain in the jungle. Here in this film, it’s the dream of an ideal country, which doesn’t really exist, the Orkneys, where real love is possible — and you would rather dig a tunnel through a whole mountain range to find this country. Everybody should dig a tunnel. Every grown-up man should move a ship over a mountain. Every grown-up woman should dig a tunnel through a mountain range. It’s very simple: Just go out and do it. That seems to have been your attitude throughout your career, given that you didn’t have a film education. HERZOG Yes, but I’m not acting blindly. I know what I’m doing. I know that I’m a poet. I dream big, but I do the doable, and that’s what I try to preach to young filmmakers. Yes, dream big, but please do the doable. Moving a ship over a mountain is doable. Digging a tunnel through a mountain is also doable. Do that. Werner Herzog shares his thoughts on Elon Musk's mission to Mars: "I am very critical of his idea of colonizing Mars with a million people. That's a pipe dream. We will have astronauts there, a handful, fine. But we should not colonize there. That's an obscenity." pic.twitter.com/B80O8jQgJG — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) September 3, 2026 What surprised you about working with him? ROONEY MARA The specificity. For some reason I imagined things would be a little bit more wild and freewheeling. I didn’t imagine the precision and specificity with which Werner works. HERZOG I interrupt and say no. Mid-take. ROONEY MARA Mid-take. Because you had something specific in mind. KATE MARA Agreed. You founded your own Rogue Film School, and you have an audience among very young, up-and-coming filmmakers. Why do you think that is? HERZOG It’s not film students alone, it’s audiences in general. They are very young. I started an Instagram account — my younger son does it, he knows how — and he tells me 85 percent of those who read it and love it are between 15 and 20 years old. Because my films are now available on the internet, on streaming platforms, all of a sudden, from one day to the next, there are 800,000 people who speak about one film of mine. There’s a film club in, God knows, Missoula, Montana, by 15-year-olds, about my films. The answer is simple: They are just very good, and they discover it. ROONEY MARA I think it’s also that you are a singular human being. You are yourself. You really don’t give a shit. You march to the beat of your own drum so thoroughly, and people love that because that’s what we all want to do. That’s what we all aspire to do. And so many of us are not doing that. HERZOG But I’m just a poet. This is the first time you two have appeared on screen together. Why did it take this long? KATE MARA It’s very difficult to find two roles that are equally interesting and good in a film, and then also find a director that we both passionately want to work with. We found all those things in this. It was really simple. Nothing came our way before that made sense in all areas. We couldn’t really believe it. What was it like to perform together as sisters? ROONEY MARA It was a very surreal experience. Strange, because it’s not like we were in scenes playing off of one another the way you normally would with a scene partner. We were playing the same thing. There’s maybe only one scene, and a few moments other than that, where we’re even looking at each other. We are focused on the same thing. It’s really one performance. KATE MARA We’re experiencing the other actor that we’re in a scene with together. So it’s impossible to compare it to anything else. We’ve never had an experience like that before. It’s great for codependency. So you’re jointly forming a single performance rather than doing two separate ones. KATE MARA It’s as collaborative as you could possibly be. HERZOG It’s unique. We haven’t seen anything like this in film history. From left: Rooney and Kate Mara in ‘Bucking Fastard.’ Gateway to Orkney You are best known for collaborations with male actors — Klaus Kinski, Christian Bale, Nicolas Cage. You’ve had a few leading female roles, but not that many. Was the approach different with these two actresses? HERZOG With every single one, with every single actor, I speak differently. I act differently. I bring them into the film, make them give the inner life of them onto a screen. There’s no school. And by the way, the greatest with whom I ever worked is the unknown soldier of cinema, Bruno S., who plays a leading part in The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser and in Stroszek . He’s the deepest, most tragic one with whom I ever worked. All of the others are actors. He was not. The film is funnier than some might expect. HERZOG Thank you that you saw it. There’s always humor in my films, and it came across, apparently. Sometimes it’s a dark humor. Sometimes it’s a very Bavarian humor that even Germans wouldn’t understand. Americans easier. Mexicans, yes, they immediately get it. Will that surprise audiences? KATE MARA Werner is one of the funniest people. If you know him and his work, or if you watch him speak about anything, he’s got the greatest sense of humor. ROONEY MARA We had so much fun. I laughed more than I have in years making this film. We had so many fun moments. Did it live up to the myth of Werner Herzog? ROONEY MARA It exceeded it. HERZOG But from the beginning I told them, I have to load an entire film onto these two shoulders, so that’s big. Are you ready for that? And of course they were. I’m a lucky man that they were immediately ready. Yes, we will carry that. You are often drawn to extreme characters, figures who exist outside of normal social structures. Is that something you see in yourself? HERZOG They’re not really borderline. Even in Bucking Fastard , I don’t see them as borderline. They make a lot of sense to me. It’s only unusual that they have apparently one dream together, one love for an undeserving man, and they speak in unison. So that’s unusual. But otherwise, they’re the most normal human creatures for me that you can imagine. They do the thing we all should do. ROONEY MARA I agree. I think everyone else is crazy. Being willing to show up every day and dig a tunnel through a mountain for love — that’s not crazy. Everyone else is crazy for not wanting to do that. HERZOG Thank you for saying that, because I keep saying I’m the only filmmaker who is clinically sane. All the rest is not really right. What can the rest of the film business learn from how he works? ROONEY MARA There’s so much you could learn from Werner. Again, it’s that willingness to show up as yourself and not be swayed by any of the noise. To have that tunnel vision of, this is who I am, and this is what I’m doing, and this is how I do it, and I’m a poet, period. KATE MARA It’s very inspiring to watch. HERZOG The work on my set is like open-heart surgery, only in whispers, going straight for the essential and nothing else. That’s it. KATE MARA You can hear a whisper from a mile away, and he will tell you so. The set is very quiet, which is great. HERZOG No cell phones, no video playout, one camera, very few takes. I do the slate. ROONEY MARA And almost no crew. He does the slate. He’s in there, crawling around within the scene. It’s very special. You’ve shot in the jungle, the desert, the Arctic Circle, and you’re still making films in your 80s. Where do you still want to explore? HERZOG I have my next film almost finished. I need a week more and my next film will be finished, so I’m way beyond Bucking Fastard . I’m also finishing a book at Taschen, the publishing house, of photos from my films. So I’m still working a lot. I love what I do. Is the dream still to go to space and make a film there? ROONEY MARA What? You want to go to space? HERZOG Yes, I would like to be out there. I have tried. I spoke to NASA, but they didn’t take me. And then there is a Japanese billionaire who is planning a spaceship around the moon, without landing, returning — he refused to take me on board. ROONEY MARA We should set up an online petition HERZOG So let’s wait. Let’s wait for the rocket for me alone. I’ll be on board. KATE MARA If anyone can do it, you can. HERZOG By the way, Elon Musk promised me that if he goes on a mission to Mars, I would be on board. But God knows when that’s happening, and I am very critical of his idea of colonizing Mars with a million people. That’s a pipe dream. We will have astronauts there, a handful at a time, and they will explore, but we should not colonize. That’s an obscenity. We should rather keep this planet inhabitable. THR

title: Rubaiyat Hossain on Bodies, Beauty and Venice, Toronto and London-Bound ‘The Difficult Bride,’ Clip Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 5, 2026 12:57am PT Rubaiyat Hossain on Bodies, Beauty and Venice, Toronto and London-Bound ‘The Difficult Bride,’ Clip Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Rubaiyat Hossain on Bodies, Beauty and Venice, Toronto and London-Bound ‘The Difficult Bride,’ Clip Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Lav Diaz Preps False Prophets Film and Jose Rizal’s ‘Noli Me Tangere’ Adaptation, Unpacks Venice Title ‘Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors’ (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Ann Hui, Carlo Chatrian to Head Pingyao’s Fei Mu, Rossellini Juries 21 hours ago See All Films Boutique The idea for “ The Difficult Bride ” traces back to a story Rubaiyat Hossain heard as a 7 year old, visiting a Dhaka beauty parlor with her mother. “There was a bride who died there,” Hossain says. “Everyone knew this story from our generation, and I remember being seven, and even at that time, I had visualized this story. It was in sepia for some reason, I don’t know, but I completely had the visuals in my head, and it’s something that always stayed with me.” Related Stories Disney Offers Executives Voluntary Early Retirement Packages Amid Overall Cost-Cutting Plans ABC Files First Amendment Lawsuit Against FCC Variety is unveiling an exclusive clip from the supernatural feminist drama, which will become the first Bangladeshi feature to screen at the Venice Film Festival when it bows in the Horizons competition. Popular on Variety That salon, Mayfair, became the setting for a film that follows Zaineen (Zaineen Chowdhury Karim), a bride-to-be whose wedding preparations spiral into a battle with her own body. Hossain first tried the material as a short in 2006. Two decades and many drafts later, the project pulled in her academic background in gender studies alongside something more personal. “My own self and my own body became a part of the film,” she says. “My embodied experience of being a female in my own body and how I feel is something I tried to communicate in the film. And that is why it became supernatural, because a lot of the things are not logical. That is where the grotesque comes in, that is where the lizards and the snakes come in.” Hossain is careful not to place the blame for that pressure solely on men. Azmeri Haque Badhon plays the salon owner who enforces the beauty standard on Zaineen, including a scene of facial injections that Hossain says mirrors treatment common in Bangladeshi salons. “It’s also about how women can be some of the biggest upholders and sustainers of patriarchy and the patriarchal system,” she says. “It’s not only men; women also participate in this. It’s a system of power. It takes both to participate in it.” The film’s Dhaka backdrop carries traces of the country’s July 2024 unrest , including scenes of women being surveilled and policed for their clothing and behavior, work that reaches the screen through Rikita Nondine Shimu’s character, Minoti. Hossain resists reading the film as a direct response to that period, though. “I wouldn’t say the film is set around the time of July,” she says. “I tried to create like a reality of Dhaka where there is political violence outside, there is a lot of violence against women. Women’s rights have always been an issue in Bangladesh.” She places “The Difficult Bride” alongside her earlier features as a kind of class trilogy of Bangladeshi womanhood. “‘Under Construction’ talked about a middle-class woman, ‘Made in Bangladesh’ talked about a working-class woman, and I think ‘The Difficult Bride’ talks about the kind of the ultra-wealthy population of the tri-state,” she says, referring to Dhaka’s Gulshan-Baridhara area. “Even in this gilded cage, even with all these privileges, you can’t be free.” Karim, making her acting debut in the lead role, was originally Hossain’s assistant director. When the shoot’s original cast changed following the disruption from July, Karim stepped in to read opposite another actor during Zoom rehearsals. “She is so beautiful and I feel like she is the character herself,” Hossain says of watching her on screen. “I might have auditioned her like around 15, 20 times.” The cast also includes Sunerah Kamal in addition to Badhon and Shimu, all three of whom are Bangladesh National Film Award winners. Hossain, who teaches part-time at Smith College, including a course on love and devotion in Bollywood cinema, argues that the pressures her film dramatizes extend well beyond South Asia. “I see that a woman who is coming from Mexico or Guatemala or Bangladesh or Vermont have same issues when it comes to this specific idea of beauty and submitting,” she says. Offscreen, Hossain has launched a grant and mentorship program for Bangladeshi women filmmakers, aiming to address what she describes as compounding structural barriers: limited access to money, restrictions on women’s mobility, the absence of a formal film school and an industry culture built on informal, male peer networks. “There is also like an overall assumption and lack of role models,” she says. “The Difficult Bride” is an international co-production between France’s Les Films de l’Après-Midi, Bangladesh’s Khona Talkies, Portugal’s Midas Filmes, Norway’s Barentsfilm and Germany’s Tandem Production, and was supported by the first edition of the Fondazione Prada Film Fund. Films Boutique is handling world sales . Following Venice, the film moves on to the Toronto and BFI London film festivals. For Hossain, the film marked a creative turning point. “I’m not tied to social realism anymore,” she says. “I really relied on my body and my instincts to make creative decisions, and I really enjoyed the process.” She is now developing a project set in Lisbon about an undocumented Bangladeshi woman who migrates after a cyclone, and is pursuing a television adaptation of J. title: Telluride Awards Analysis: Andrew Scott Leaps Into Top Tier of Best Actor Oscar Race for ‘Elsinore’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All September 5, 2026 12:21am Andrew Scott in 'Elsinore' Courtesy of StudioCanal With all due respect to the performances of Matt Damon in The Odyssey and Ryan Gosling in Project Hail Mary , I came away from Wild Horse Nine , which had its North American premiere at the Telluride Film Festival on Thursday afternoon, with the strong impression that John Malkovich was now the clear frontrunner to win the best actor Oscar. But by Friday evening, when Elsinore had its world premiere in Telluride, I was forced to revise my hypothesis. That’s because the Irish actor Andrew Scott gives a performance for the ages in Elsinore as the Scottish actor Ian Charleson, who was best known for starring in the best picture Oscar winner Chariots of Fire , but whose most impressive accomplishment was how he insisted on continuing to act — in the role of Hamlet at London’s National Theatre, no less — even after he was diagnosed with terminal AIDS. Related Stories Movies 'Elsinore' Review: Andrew Scott Is Shattering as British Actor Ian Charleson, Throwing Himself Into Playing Hamlet While Succumbing to AIDS Movies 'The Idiot(s)' Review: Aimee Lou Wood and Johnny Flynn Sparkle in a Playful, Indulgent Tribute to Fyodor Dostoevsky's Underappreciated Wife The response inside Telluride’s Palm Theatre to the listing of Scott’s name in the film’s post-credits — as both a producer and the lead actor — was undeniable. It’s a sensitive and shattering performance from an actor who just keeps getting better, as demonstrated in everything from his film performance in All of Us Strangers , which premiered in Telluride three years ago, to his stage performance last year in Uncle Vanya , in which he singlehandedly juggled 10 different characters. In the Oscar race, Malkovich could have a slight edge because he’s older (73 versus 49), because he has been doing important work for longer and because his film is all but certain to land noms in a bunch of categories, including best picture, whereas aspects of Elsinore other than Scott’s performance are more of a question-mark. I wouldn’t count out the possibility of noms for Olivia Colman for best supporting actress (she plays Charleson’s doctor), Stephen Beresford’s script for best original screenplay (even though the film’s credits say it was inspired by “an idea” from someone else), Valerio Bonelli’s film editing (particularly awesome late in the film as he cuts between Charleson on stage and at home), Stefan Gregory’s original score or even the film for a best picture nom. But the truth is that Scott’s performance is so extraordinary that other aspects of the Simon Stone’s film — which The Hollywood Reporter ’s critic has argued is solid but less spectacular — could be overshadowed. One final note. Quite a few actors and actresses have won Oscars for their portrayals of LGBT characters facing adversity and/or tragedy, including William Hurt for Kiss of the Spider Woman , Tom Hanks for Philadelphia , Hilary Swank for Boys Don’t Cry , Sean Penn for Milk , Jared Leto for Dallas Buyers Club and Rami Malek for Bohemian Rhapsody . But none of those people were themselves gay, and indeed never has an out gay actor or actress won an Oscar. Scott could well become the first. THR

title: Lee Chang-dong On His Eight-Year Hiatus & Confident Return With Venice Competition Title ‘Possible Love’
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Lee Chang-dong On His Eight-Year Hiatus & Confident Return With Venice Competition Title ‘Possible Love’ Ira Sachs To Preside Over San Sebastián’s Competition Jury Theo Rollason On How He Discovered 30 Hours Of Behind-The-Scenes Derek Jarman Footage To Create ‘Queer Edward II’ — Venice View All September 5, 2026 12:21am Sul Kyung-gu as Ho-seok, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok in 'Possible Love.' Joo Jae-bum/Netflix © 2026 Lee Chang-dong has finally returned to feature filmmaking. The Korean filmmaker has been on an extended eight-year hiatus, which he blames on his “pathological timidity.” “Unless I have that conviction, I cannot make myself begin the work, no matter the external circumstances or what others around me say,” he tells Deadline via Zoom from his office in Korea , ahead of his trip to Venice , where, this weekend, his latest film Possible Love , a title full of conviction but also comedy and sharp social critique, debuts in Competition. Related Stories News Loco Films Boards Venice Title 'Guria' As Drama Is Selected To Be Georgia's Oscar Entry + First Trailer News MAD Solutions & IRTH Strike Pan-Arab Development & Production Strategic Partnership - Venice Director Lee helmed the film from a screenplay he co-wrote with Oh Jung-mi. The pair previously worked together on Chang-dong’s last film, the excellent Burning (2018). The story follows two married couples whose lives become uniquely intertwined. There is Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), who lives a quiet life with her husband, Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), and their young son Cheol. Watch on Deadline Ho-seok has been laid off from his job following an incident that has stunted his life and his ability to communicate with his family. We only learn what that incident was after the family meets Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a documentary filmmaker engaged in a project about the lives of laid-off workers, and her ultra-wealthy husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). When Mi-ok agrees to be filmed, she grows close to Ye-ji, creating an uncomfortable friction that shakes both of their households. Running just short of three hours, Possible Love is a masterful return by Chang-dong. Below, the filmmaker, joined by one of his leading men, Sul Kyung-gu, discusses why it has taken him almost a decade to make Possible Love . The filmmaker says he initially shelved the project, fearing he wasn’t the most suitable messenger for a film about labor rights. Chang-dong also explains why there is a tribute to Krzysztof Kieślowski’s Dekalog at the end of Possible Love , and why he believes so many contemporary Korean filmmakers have been so successful at interrogating the relationship or, as the Marxists would say, struggle between labor and capital in their work. Netflix will release Possible Love in cinemas on October 23. The film hits the streamer on November 6. DEADLINE: Director Lee, where did this idea come from? LEE CHANG-DONG: Some years ago in Korea, a Korean conglomerate went through mass layoffs. That was met with an all-or-nothing strike from the labor side. There was also a merciless crackdown by the authorities. At the time, I remember thinking it would be a transformative event in the Korean labor market. I also knew it probably meant the beginning of a normalization of such restructuring of conglomerates that would greatly change the lives of these laborers. I wrote a screenplay, but at the last minute, I started to ask myself: Am I worthy of telling a story like this? I mean, do I have the right? Documentaries had already been filmed about the subject. Could I really justify turning this into a dramatic film? I couldn’t get a clear answer to that question, so I shelved the project. A lot of time passed, and then my co-writer, Oh Jung-mi, came up with the idea of telling this story alongside the tale of a documentary filmmaker. That got me thinking I could do this project. And that led me to revisit the project. Sul Kyung-gu as Ho-seok, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok, Cho Yeo-jeong as Ye-ji, Zo In-sung as Sang-woo in ‘Possible Love’. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026. DEADLINE: I went in blind, so the documentary element really surprised me. What do you want people to take away from that aspect of this story? CHANG-DONG: This is the story of all people who make films, no matter what kind of film it is. It could be a genre film or a dramatic film. As filmmakers, we deal with and portray people’s lives, and therefore, we are bound to be strongly connected to social issues. And as we deal with the pain of others, we must think: are we really making sure to treat them as we would our own, candidly and honestly? Or are we just consuming it to make our films? This question is inseparable from the work for those of us who create films. That’s why I wanted to take that question and expand it, not only in relation to creators but also to audiences. I hope they can think about their relationship with themselves and others. DEADLINE: Sul, you’ve worked with Director Lee before. When did you first hear about this project? SUL KYUNG-GU: I first heard about Possible Love last March. Director Lee and I met about two years ago, at the end of 2024, and he didn’t mention a new project. In fact, when we’re together, we still often meet with fans of our previous film, Peppermint Candy . A few months after that meeting, he reached out to me and told me about Possible Love . At the time, I was perplexed because I was already attached to a different project, but I knew I had to make this work. I spoke with the other director and begged him. Finally, they made it work for me. The actual story and meaning of Possible Love wasn’t even important to me. What was important to me was working with director Lee Chang-dong again. I didn’t even ask to see the screenplay. Director Lee actually asked me, “Hey, you’re not even interested in reading the screenplay at all?” When I first read it, it just felt like a Lee Chang-dong script. It quite literally smelled of him. It had his fragrance. When you get something that Director Lee writes, it concerns you in the sense that you really want to make it work and do it well. DEADLINE: Director Lee, people have been anticipating your next film for some time now. It has been almost a decade since Burning. Do you ever feel anxiety about that anticipation? CHANG-DONG: I remember promising people after Burning that my next film would not take as long. But regretfully, I wasn’t able to keep that promise. I did have many people reach out to me asking when I would make my next film. I think that you could almost say it’s an obsessive side of me, almost a pathological timidity or whatnot. But unless I have that conviction, I cannot make myself begin the work, no matter the external circumstances or what others around me say. Zo In-sung as Sang-woo, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok in ‘Possible Love’ Credit: Joo Jae-bum/Netflix © 2026 DEADLINE: The music in this film is wonderful. Jung Jaeil, who has previously worked with Director Bong and Kore-eda, worked on the score. How did you two work together? CHANG-DONG: I have never been a fan of using a lot of music in my films. This is just something that I carry as a filmmaker. I feel like the music tends to emphasize emotions outside the film, and I believe the musicality of the films should lie within the film itself. And so I shared these thoughts with Jung Jaeil. I told him that I would like the music to be limited to a minimum yet still convey the film’s structure and emotions to the audience. He understood me completely, and I really think that the results he came up with were just right. DEADLINE: There’s a tribute to Kieślowski’s Dekalog at the end of this movie. This isn’t an adaptation from that film series. What is the connection? CHANG-DONG: When I was writing this script, Kieślowski’s Dekalog was being adapted into a new project, with different feature films being assigned to each of the series. I was offered the chance to take part in the project. This film is unrelated to the Dekalog one, but I thought I could integrate the commandment they were dealing with in that film into this story: the 10th commandment, “Thou shalt not covet”. All the other nine commandments are about human action. However, the 10th commandment is all about human desire, so I thought that in today’s capitalist world, we could really deal with the question: can we truly live without coveting others’ lives? DEADLINE: You mention today’s capitalist world. Can you both tell me: Why are so many Korean filmmakers able to so skilfully and powerfully deal with our relationship to labor and capital in their films? CHANG-DONG: That’s something I’m personally curious about as well. But what I can say is that it goes to show just how rapid an economic change and development the Korean society has experienced over the past decades. Just a few decades ago, Korea experienced a tremendous war. We were one of the poorest countries in the world, and within a few decades we achieved very rapid economic development. However, as a result, we had to pay a grave social cost, and I believe the aftermath of that change is deeply rooted in our society. Within that process, we also experienced a political change, which led to conflict about academia and intellectuals. This has all been engraved in the Korean people, and I believe it is why we deal with these issues in such a serious manner. We carry it all with us in our everyday lives. KYUNG-GU: I agree. It is a result of the rapid change our society went through and the intense conflict that led to it. And I think we are going to have a lot more stories to come going forward as well. ‘Brand New Day’ Owning Labor Day Frame, Nears ‘Force Awakens’ For U.S. No. 1 ‘Elsinore’ & Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ Reviews; Inside ‘In The Breach’ ‘Spider-Noir’ Canceled As Prime Video Eyes Another Sony/Marvel Series Zach Cregger Talks ‘Resident Evil’, Drive To Work With Spielberg & More Read More About: Comments

News of the acquisition follows hot on the heels of Georgia ’s decision to submit the feature as its entry to the 99th Academy Awards . Set in the director’s native western Georgia, the film follows Zuriko, a 45-year-old hazelnut farmer navigating the economic challenges, romantic adventures and the surreal realities of life in the post-Soviet village of Guria. Meanwhile, his best friend Gela attempts to find him a new wife, introducing him to a string of potential matches, none of whom win the approval of Zuriko’s formidable ex-mother-in-law. “ Guria is about ordinary people who live under harsh conditions yet manage to preserve their humanity,” Koguashvili said. “It is a natural cradle of tragicomedy, the genre I love most.” Beyond being the film’s geographical setting, director Koguashvili describes western Georgia as “a state of mind,” adding he wanted to make a film about ordinary people without ideological or political agendas. “Just pure living. title: ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Shattering as British Actor Ian Charleson, Throwing Himself Into Playing Hamlet While Succumbing to AIDS
full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 10:00pm Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman in 'Elsinore.' Anthony Dickenson/Focus Features The late British stage and screen actor Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS-related causes in 1990 at age 40, is mostly remembered for his role in the 1981 Oscar winner Chariots of Fire . That inescapable attachment haunts Charleson, played with raw determination, grace and an almost overwhelming depth of feeling by Andrew Scott in Elsinore , a tremendously moving account of the final year in the Scottish actor’s life. When his agent reminds him that he starred in one of the most celebrated films of all time, Charleson shoots back: “And all anybody can remember about it is the theme music.” Related Stories Movies 'A Long Winter' Review: Fred Hechinger and Ebon Moss-Bachrach Shine as Family Thrust Into Uneasy Isolation in Andrew Haigh's Fine-Grained Drama Movies 'Tender Loving Care' Review: Kate O'Flynn Lights Up Mike Leigh's Warm, Gently Wrenching Study of Solace and Solidarity Scott’s searing dual performance — as Charleson and as Hamlet in a National Theatre production that became both the ultimate challenge and fulfillment of his professional career — makes Simon Stone ’s film an emotional powerhouse even if it doesn’t avoid inspirational cliché. But it’s a vivid picture of London at the height of the AIDS crisis and a stirring gesture of gratitude to art, specifically theater, as a lifeline even when death looms large. Elsinore The Bottom Line A hymn to the theater powered by a towering lead turn. Venue : Telluride Film Festival Release date : Friday, Nov. 20 Cast : Andrew Scott, Olivia Colman, Billie Piper, Johnny Flynn, Luke Thompson, David Dawson, Matthew Beard, Joe Locke, Monica Dolan, Georgie Glen, Sadie Soverall, Juliet Stevenson, Peter Mullan Director : Simon Stone Screenwriter : Stephen Beresford 1 hour 51 minutes While Charleson’s heroic run of 24 performances in the title role of Hamlet is as much a part of London theater lore as the abrupt exit from Richard Eyre ’s 1989 production of Daniel Day-Lewis , it will be less familiar to audiences farther afield. The script by Stephen Beresford ( Pride ) lives and breathes the stage community and its cozy familial camaraderie, from actors and directors to wardrobe, makeup and tech personnel. The bustle of theater luvvies all fondly addressing one another as “darling” will be especially amusing for audiences with any exposure to that world. As a film about a painful chapter in queer history, it mines considerable humor from the extent to which gay slang seeps into the entire milieu, regardless of sexuality. One hilarious example is Monica Dolan, marvelous as Linda Tolhurst, the National’s stage door supervisor for 50 years and counting. Charleson was already chummy with the building’s fixtures after playing Sky Masterson in the company’s smash 1982 Guys and Dolls revival; when he arrives for the first table read after being cast to replace Day-Lewis as Hamlet, Linda greets him dryly with, “’Ere she is, Takeover Tina!” While Charleson initially established himself as a stage actor, his primary international recognition came from back-to-back best picture Oscar winners Chariots of Fire and Gandhi . But despite working steadily, he struggled to keep the momentum of a screen career going. Growing tired of all the waiting around on film shoots for mostly unrewarding projects, Charleson became anxious to get back to the theater, especially given the ticking clock of his HIV+ diagnosis. Stone’s film shows the confusion of backstage workers and fellow cast when Day-Lewis collapses and then walks offstage during the Act I scene on the castle ramparts in which Hamlet encounters his father’s ghost. While the screenplay doesn’t go into the then-rising star’s reasons for abandoning the production, it’s no secret that Day-Lewis was unsettled by a connection to his own father’s absence, even if his exit was widely attributed to exhaustion. That footnote in London theater history creates an opportunity for Charleson, who previously played Hamlet though believed he was neither famous nor posh enough ever to land the role at the National. When he is approached by Eyre — identified only as Richard ( Johnny Flynn ) — who had directed him in Guys and Dolls , Ian feels duty-bound to inform him of his medical condition. The first appearance of a lesion on his forehead — after inspecting every inch of his body with a hand mirror each day — marked Ian’s progression to full-blown AIDS. Richard automatically assumes he will be unable to take on the demanding role, but Ian’s passion and drive convince him, with both men agreeing to keep his illness quiet. A lovely scene on cruisy Hampstead Heath takes creative license with the formation of the London chapter of the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence, drag nuns advocating for AIDS awareness and safer sex practices. (In reality, that group didn’t appear in the British capital until the early ‘90s.) Ian asks Sister Frigidity of the Nocturnal Emission (Kadiff Kirwan) how long he has left, prompting the veiled activist to summon a young man from elsewhere in the park, still alive two years after his first lesion appeared. Instantly recognizing the mark on Charleson’s face for what it is, the National’s wardrobe master (Paul Chahidi) sends him to see Dr. Margaret Johnson ( Olivia Colman ), a U.K. pioneer of HIV and AIDS treatment. Colman is in blazing form, her clipped manner contrasting with the medic’s self-evident compassion. Instructing Ian to start coming for daily clinic checkups, she makes no effort to hide her anger that the actor is increasing his risk of decline by placing himself in a high-pressure situation. Developments with the terse character later in the film are profoundly affecting. Scenes at the clinic, where gay men constantly encounter friends and ex-lovers receiving treatment at various stages of the illness, are a sharp evocation of a time when the proliferation of men looking suddenly gaunt and weak sparked terror in the entire queer community. Charleson’s vibrantly drawn inner circle of friends is led by his bestie, casting director Patsy Pollock ( Billie Piper ), her daughter Alice (Sadie Soverall) and his constant companion Sean (Matthew Beard). The latter is identified, like Eyre, only by his first name, but the character is based on Sean Mathias, who directed Charleson that year in an all-star benefit performance of Martin Sherman’s play Bent , about pink-triangle persecution in Nazi Germany. One of the most fascinating insights into queer history comes with the appearances of iconoclastic director Derek Jarman (David Dawson), a friend for whom Charleson had played a punk angel in 1978’s Jubilee . As his own illness progresses, Derek urges Ian to go public about his health, to help destigmatize AIDS and hammer home the reality of the plague for Brits outside of LGBTQ circles. This brings up the conflicts for gay actors at the time who felt the need to keep their sexuality hidden for fear of career damage. “You have a responsibility to the dead, to the dying,” Derek tells him. Reflecting on his choice to stay silent (until after his death) Ian says, “Of course, in the theater no one gives a fuck.” But there was more at stake back then — and still to some extent now — for actors seeking on-camera work. For anyone who recalls Jarman’s seismic influence on queer cinema with uncompromising films like Sebastiane , The Angelic Conversation , Caravaggio and Edward II , hearing the director say “Ian, remember me” with the knowledge that any encounter could be their last cuts deep. The same goes for Charleson visiting him at the fisherman’s cottage in coastal Dungeness where he lived at the time, when Jarman tells him that he’s going blind. His loss of vision shaped his experimental swan-song feature, 1993’s Blue . If all this makes Elsinore sound like a film primarily for a niche audience of queer historians, that’s not the case. As Charleson digs into Hamlet rehearsals, insisting on working late even when he’s physically diminished, Scott conveys the actor’s dedication to his craft with both self-sacrifice and hubris. As Richard says of the play: “It’s about being alive and becoming dead.” While Stone is not always the most subtle of directors and Beresford’s dialogue often doesn’t tread lightly, a scene in which Ian gathers the entire cast to give an honest account of his condition — after being forced into a hiatus when he is hospitalized during previews — is as heartwarming as it is wrenching. But it’s in the performance scenes that Scott truly elevates the material, drawing on intersections between the Shakespearean role and Ian’s own thoughts of mortality. Many audiences will be wrecked by pretty much the entire second half of the movie, the final scenes in particular, in which editor Valerio Bonelli crosscuts between the stage performance and Ian’s bedroom at home, where he is fading fast, comforted by Patsy. When Laertes tells the wounded prince at the end of the Act 5 sword fight, “Hamlet, thou art slain,” I was a mess. While the fire at the core of the film is all Scott, in a physical, psychological and emotional performance that leaves nothing on the table, there’s gorgeous work throughout the ensemble. Colman superbly nails the seeming contradiction between professional medical detachment and humaneness. Piper — whom Stone directed on stage to huge acclaim on both sides of the Atlantic in his adaptation of Lorca’s Yerma — embodies the cherished female friend who is a sustaining force in the lives of so many gay men. And an unrecognizable Flynn makes Eyre a shining example of the director as nurturer and protector. There are standout moments for Luke Thompson as Georgie, a composite character representing Ian’s past relationships; Juliet Stevenson as Sylvia Sims, portrayed as a grand dame of British thespianism while playing Gertrude in the National production; Beard as a friend whose selfless devotion to Ian’s care is on par with Patsy’s; and Heartstopper ’s Joe Locke as an admiring young actor hungry for mentorship, befriended by Ian at the clinic. The most devastating scenes for many will be those with Ian’s parents, Jean (Georgie Glen) and Jack (Peter Mullan), working-class Scots confronted with the double whammy that their son is not only gay but dying, a confessional ordeal common to many AIDS patients at the time. Both actors are wonderful, with Jean’s anguish immediately apparent and Jack’s sputtering to the surface in a delayed reaction in the hospital car park. It’s a nice touch that one of Charleson’s surviving Chariots of Fire castmates, Nigel Havers, pops up as an AIDS clinic donor, alongside Ian’s close friend and University of Edinburgh classmate, fellow actor Hilton McRae. The latter is the longtime husband of Lindsay Duncan, Charleson’s co-star in a landmark 1988 National Theatre production of Cat on a Hot Tin Roof . There’s a nice “friends and family” aspect to these and other connections. Whatever weaknesses there are in the direction and script, the film makes enormous gains in intimacy and authenticity by eliminating any of the barriers of outsider observation. The full-throated investment in the parallel queer, theatrical, medical and outpatient communities is unquestionably personal. Stone relies more than necessary on Stefan Gregory’s lush orchestral score to push emotional buttons. But the strategic use in one joyously tender scene of The Ethel Merman Disco Album — once a cringey embarrassment, now a beloved bit of queer pop cultural kitsch — will spark fun associations for many gay men over a certain age. The Merm belting out “There’s No Business Like Show Business” to a disco backbeat might be a million brassy miles from Shakespeare, but Elsinore lovingly folds those two extremes together. title: ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Kate O’Flynn Stars In What Could Be Mike Leigh’s Final Film, But It Happens To Be One Of His Best – Telluride Film Festival View All September 4, 2026 10:00pm Andrew Scott in 'Elsinore' Focus Features Scottish-born actor Ian Charleson co-starred in a leading role in the 1981 Oscar-winning Best Picture Chariots of Fire. The next year he had a co-starring role in yet another Best Picture winner, Gandhi. Not bad, but in his heart he was an actor born to the London stage, and as the Hollywood career faded he was frustrated being offered lesser kinds of films and TV roles, or only being known for one movie with an iconic musical theme. By the end of the decade that started with such promise, Charleson was diagnosed with HIV/AIDS at a time when it was difficult as an actor to be honest and share the truth. Although he knew he was dying, he was still full of life with a passion for theater and for living onstage. Fate intervened, and Daniel Day-Lewis dropped out of the British National Theatre’s production of Hamlet , walking off in the middle of the play. The production’s director knew Charleson’s work well and offered him the part. Aside from a very few people including the director Richard Eyre, no one knew Charleson was doing this role against all odds. Like the theme of a play about choosing life or death, “to be or not to be,” a real-life drama was also playing out in the 24 performances Charleson managed to play despite full-blown AIDS, chemotherapy and a doctor who warned he was killing himself. He would die at age 40 seven weeks after the production ended. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Festivals ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival Festivals Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’ Makes Tabloid Headlines At Telluride Stephen Beresford had always known Charleson’s inspirational story, talked to many people who were there at the time and knew him, and wrote the screenplay for Elsinore that is not a biopic at all but rather a film about the end of a life, though not the end of living. Director Simon Stone and Beresford have crafted an immensely inspirational and winning film quite unlike most other movies set around the AIDS crisis that took so many young lives. This, like Hamlet , is about staring death in the face and fulfilling a dream not thought impossible. What Elsinore, which had its world premiere Friday night at the Telluride Film Festival, has above all else is a performance for the ages by Andrew Scott , an actor fully embodying the heart and soul of another actor and finding the emotional center and determination to take this last chance no matter what the cost. It is something Charleson, even at the lowest point of his illness, just had to do, and Scott delivers at every level with a portrayal that is (there is no other word for it) thrilling . The movie is also a love letter to Britain’s National Theatre, a sprawling monument to the power of art and artists, an “Elsinore” unto itself. Ironically also debuting at the Telluride Film Festival this weekend is the stunning documentary on the history of The National, Into the Breach, featuring interviews with key players from Ian McKellen and Joan Plowright to Eddie Redmayne. Kenneth Branagh, who co-produced, anchors it with a roundtable featuring the likes of Judi Dench, Anthony Hopkins and Gary Oldman. In no particular order, Elsinore darts in and out of various phases of Charleson’s life during this period, but Stone manages the tonal balance expertly. We see Ian’s interactions with friends and those in the gay community also stricken with AIDS, the deaths of some, his frustration with his stalled career, his mad desire to play Hamlet, his interactions with the medical staff and the key doctor who fought to keep him alive, his parents, the rehearsals, his worsening condition and hospitalization, his remission, and finally the performance. It is also expertly cut (the fine editing is by Valerio Banelli) and keeps the focus on this spirited man tilting at windmills, showing great courage and grit all the way. We also see the unique traditions and importance of The National to the British theater nicely re-created here (Helen Scott is the production designer). And a lip-sync dance of the hospital patients to a cassette of “There’s No Business Like Show Business” from The Ethel Merman Disco Album is worth the price of admission and proof this movie is not the downer it could have been. Instead, it thrives with heart and humanity throughout. There is a line in the film about the unique power of actors on a stage, a talent that can’t be underestimated, and in the casting of this film that is clear. Scott owns every moment, but he is supported by a tremendous ensemble starting with the great Olivia Colman as Dr. Margaret Johnson, a pioneer in the treatment of AIDS and the doctor who tried to keep it real with Ian but eventually learned it was a losing proposition to fight his dream. Colman is magnificent here getting to the essence of what makes a compassionate healer as she does everything she can to keep Ian alive and able to perform, no matter how dangerous. As his good friend and confidante Patsy Pollock, the person who encourages him to get back onstage but also who knows the cost, Billie Piper is wonderful, as are Peter Mullan as his distraught father; Juliet Stevenson as an empathetic co-star; and Johnny Flynn as Eyre, the director who gives him this opportunity to replace Day-Lewis even after Ian reveals the condition that could make this all a risk. Luke Thomson as a close dying friend, and Joe Locke as a young patient who idolizes Ian and wants career advice he will never be able to use, are both heartbreaking. David Dawson is superb as the director Derek Jarman. who gave Ian an early break and now chastises him for not going public. They share one of the film’s best-written scenes as Ian explains the role of an actor is to become someone else, not to let their own life turn up onstage. In the end though it is Scott triumphing here in a film that should make you sad but smartly doesn’t dwell on death, only life as we live it. It is the role of a lifetime playing someone getting the chance to play their role of a lifetime, which is saying a lot since Scott was equally brilliant earlier this year as another real-life person, a reluctant WWII hero, in Pressure. Here he has given Ian Charleson a gift: another moment in the spotlight at the National, this time to share it with the entire world. I would recommend bringing along a value-sized box of tissues. You might need them all. Producers are Andrea Occhipinti (Lucky Red), Gabrielle Tana (Magnolia Mae Films), Pete Shilaimon (LD Entertainment), Mickey Liddell (LD Entertainment), Stefano Massenzi, Carolyn Marks Blackwood (Magnolia Mae Films) and Scott. title: ‘The Idiot(s)’ Review: Aimee Lou Wood and Johnny Flynn Sparkle in a Playful, Indulgent Tribute to Fyodor Dostoevsky’s Underappreciated Wife
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 9:30pm 'The Idiot(s)' Zuzanna Woinska / Gold Rush Pictures / Hype Studios As she finishes transcribing what will become one of her husband’s most enduring masterpieces, Anna Dostoevskaya ( Aimee Lou Wood ) cannot contain her excitement: “This is our best novel yet!” She quickly corrects herself, of course — “I mean, your best novel” — but by then, we understand she had it right the first time. Sure, those might be Fyodor’s words on the page, and his name on the cover. But as Malgorzata Szumowska and Michal Englert’s shrewd, playful The Idiot(s) reminds us, not even singular geniuses really do it all alone. If the film ultimately overstays its welcome, it’s hard to fault it for wanting to let this unsung companion luxuriate, for once, in the spotlight. Related Stories Movies 'A Long Winter' Review: Fred Hechinger and Ebon Moss-Bachrach Shine as Family Thrust Into Uneasy Isolation in Andrew Haigh's Fine-Grained Drama Movies 'Tender Loving Care' Review: Kate O'Flynn Lights Up Mike Leigh's Warm, Gently Wrenching Study of Solace and Solidarity The Idiot(s) The Bottom Line Sharp and fun, even if it overstays its welcome. Venue: Telluride Film Festival Cast: Aimee Lou Wood, Johnny Flynn, Vicky Krieps, Christian Freidel Directors: Malgorzata Szumowska, Michal Englert Screenwriters: Malgorzata Szumowska, Michal Englert, Kasper Bajon, Brid Arnstein 2 hours As Anna, Wood projects both unpolished brightness and an impressive force of will; it’s a mesmerizing combination that keeps the character from ever feeling like a mere victim of her circumstances, even as her life takes the harsh turns of, well, a Russian novel. If anything, the character’s initial introduction calls to mind Wood’s earlier breakout role on The White Lotus . Here as there, she’s the sweetly enthusiastic romantic partner to a grumpy older dude who seems determined to hate the new country they’re visiting from the moment he sets foot on it. It’s just that in this case, her S.O. is not some revenge-driven man of mystery but a writer drowning in debt and stymied by writer’s block. But The Idiot(s) makes clear right away that it isn’t interested in the usual serious biopic clichés about serious men doing serious things. This Fyodor, played by Johnny Flynn as a comically exasperating combination of buffoonish confidence, abject self-pity and childish petulance, is first seen glowering at a woman peeling hard-boiled eggs on the train, a fantastically overwrought classical soundtrack underlining the unreasonable intensity of his moods. He says things like “Tolstoy’s gonna shit himself” (of the novel he, Fyodor, is definitely for sure gonna start writing any day now) and “Kick me in the face” (to Anna, as part of a kinky foot-fetish debasement ritual). It’s not that the filmmakers doubt his talent as an author — the caption to that aforementioned opener, “9 a.m., the last days of November, during the thaw,” is the first of multiple affectionate nods to Dostoevsky’s The Idiot — so much as they recognize that reverence for a person’s work need not necessarily translate to admiration for his personality. The couple have arrived in Germany ostensibly so Fyodor can work on his next project. The creatively tortured, easily distracted Fyodor, quicky sets about doing anything but. When he’s not out partying with the very upper-crust literati he claims to disdain, including rival scribe Ivan Turgenev (Christian Friedel) and his coquettish girlfriend ( Vicky Krieps , alluring but underused), he’s blowing all his money at the roulette table. When he is at home, he oscillates between drunken glee and utter despair. Whenever Anna sneaks a peek at his notebooks, she finds either blank pages or doodles of naked women, not a word of The Idiot in sight. It would all be very depressing for poor Anna, were it not for the fact that The Idiot(s) does its best to keep the phrase “poor Anna” from entering your mind for as long as it can. For one thing, the film is too busy having fun to let itself stew in misery. It’s stuffed with mischievous anachronisms like a 19th-century performance of “Take On Me,” the A-Ha hit whose pleading lyrics could double Fyodor’s entreaty to a fed-up Anna. And it delights in outrageous rococo details, like a restaurant dessert that’s essentially chocolate mousse being squeezed out the anus of a porcelain dog. More crucially, the screenplay, by Szumowska, Englert, Kasper Bajon and Brid Arnstein, paints Anna not as some passive observer to Fyodor’s bad behavior but an active (albeit only fitfully successful) guardrail against it. As her husband gives himself over to his worst impulses, it’s Anna who nudges him to work, who tries to get the bills paid, who even, as things get dire, secretly writes and submits pages on his behalf to mollify his angry publisher. While Anna may not always be in control of her own fate, there’s never any doubt she’s in possession of her own agency. True, she’s making the choices she does in part because she has few others: Living in a foreign land without even enough cash for a train ticket home, Anna would have a tough time leaving Fyodor even if she’d wanted to. But, The Idiot(s) makes it clear, she doesn’t especially want to. Anna loves Fyodor truly and stubbornly, and he loves her back in his own inconsistent and imperfect way. Key to the film’s portrait of their marriage is the frisky chemistry that courses between them when they’re holding hands in bed or engaging in silly dirty talk about hard-boiled eggs. For all the relationship’s intolerable flaws and harrowing lows, it’s not without true affection. Anna’s indulgence for his antics is another thing, however. As the situation deteriorates to the point that Anna’s pawning off her chamber pots and eating scraps off the streets, it becomes harder and harder for us as viewers to forgive his sins. Perhaps that’s why The Idiot(s) gives over large chunks of its bleaker second half to absurd dream sequences. But arriving as they do in the umpteenth iteration of the same repetitive cycle (Fyodor losing his money, begging Anna for more, losing it all again and then some), these sequences land not only as unnecessary drags on an already puffy run time but as an uncharacteristic failure of confidence. We don’t require a clip of Fyodor fleeing from a boulder-sized roulette ball to tell us he’s being crushed by his gambling addiction when we’ve already seen that he is; we don’t need to see him plead against charges of chauvinism before a guillotine when we know exactly how poorly he treats Anna. Then again, if the clunky pacing of the film’s latter chapters remind us of anything, it’s how long Anna toiled to help bring The Idiot into the world. Compared to all those long years, what’s a few extra minutes of sitting and watching her struggles on a screen? “Every Russian writer should have a wife like you,” Ivan marvels at one point, moved by Anna’s strenuous efforts to help her ungrateful and oblivious husband. What The Idiot(s) impishly suggests, by demonstrating all the invisible but essential labor Anna’s poured into his books, is that a lot of them probably already did. title: Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’ Makes Tabloid Headlines At Telluride
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew ‘The Row’ First Look: Oscar Winner Bryan Fogel Documents One Man’s Incredible Solo Row From California To Australia – Telluride Film Festival Telluride First Look: In Documentary ‘Zero Intention Of Living Quietly,’ Actor Adam Pearson Claims His Space POV Shorts Acquires Oscar Contender ‘The Boys And The Bees’; RaMell Ross, Stacey Reiss Join As EPs View All September 4, 2026 9:11pm Guy Pearce (left) as Rupert Murdoch and Jack O'Connell as Larry Lamb in 'Ink' Netflix Fresh from the Venice Film Festival where he unveiled Ink , director Danny Boyle arrived in Telluride for the North American premiere of his drama about Rupert Murdoch’s launch of the British Tabloid The Sun in 1969. Boyle, looking none the worse for international travel, introduced the film Friday night by noting that some people are misinterpreting the title. “It’s not a movie about tattoos,” he informed the Telluride audience, “which a lot of people assume it is.” Related Stories Reviews ‘Ink’ Review: Danny Boyle’s Sensational Look At The Origins Of Rupert Murdoch’s The Sun Is Also A Warning For Now – Venice Film Festival News Baz Bamigboye Looks Back On True Tabloid Life With ‘Ink’ Director Danny Boyle & Writer James Graham – Venice Film Festival The ink in question here refers to the substance necessary to print newspapers by the millions. Australian native Guy Pearce stars as Australian native Murdoch, the media baron (dubbed “the Dirty Digger” by his British rivals), who took a lightly regarded broadsheet and turned it into the UK’s most popular rag. His key move was to recruit Larry Lamb as editor, a talented if perhaps overlooked veteran of Fleet Street, the traditional home of British newspapering. Jack O’Connell stars in that lead role. Guy Pearce (left) and Jack O’Connell go face to face in ‘Ink.’ Netflix Boyle introduced O’Connell, saying, “I’d worked with this guy on 28 Years Later , but he was in a tiny bit at the end of the film, a really daft bit at the end of the film… And I wanted to work with him so much.” Watch on Deadline Netflix In his review , Deadline’s Pete Hammond calls Boyle “the perfect filmmaker to bring this world to life. It’s set in 1969 London as the brash if trash visionary Murdoch and his handpicked editor-in-chief set out to turn a flop into a top that eventually would bleed into the entire world. It’s an era before the internet and social media demanded faster and furiouser hits and clickbait to get attention, when people got their news by picking sides.” Hammond continues, “Adapted by James Graham from his Tony- and Olivier-winning 2018 play, Boyle has created a bright, fast-paced and lively film that matches the energy this band of questionable warriors had just after man first walk on the moon — perhaps triggering something that in different ways would turn out to be just as significant in the long run.” The audience awaits the start of ‘Ink’ at the Werner Herzog Theater in Telluride. Matthew Carey Ink , which will be premiere on Netlix in January, played at the Werner Herzog Theater in Telluride (ironically, Herzog himself has been busy in Venice, premiering his latest drama Bucking Fastard , starring Rooney and Kate Mara). “I’ve never been in the Werner Herzog Theater, and that is a privilege beyond belief,” the Oscar-winning director said. “But even beyond that, to be showing a film in a theater named after him, is to be part of the Telluride Festival… When you make a film, you feel lost a lot of the time. It’s a weird thing because when you appear promoting it, you look full of confidence, but you feel lost [while making it]. And when you get signals that someone might like the film, it means so much to you. And Julie [Huntsinger, executive director of Telluride] was the first to ring up and to say she was going to invite it to Telluride. And I cannot tell you what it’s like. It’s the rush of the ocean to the heart for a filmmaker. So, bless you, Julie, and bless you, Telluride.” Boyle evidently is carving out time to see some other films while in Telluride. “Was anybody at the Wild Horse Nine screening?” he asked the crowd. “There was a competition for a free holiday in Mallorca before that film. Well, there’s nothing for you [here]. I’m so sorry. title: Victor Miller, ‘Friday the 13th’ Screenwriter, Dies at 86
full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 4, 2026 8:33pm Victor Miller Instagram Victor Miller, the screenwriter behind Friday the 13th , has died. He was 86. Miller died Monday, his son, Ian, announced in a post on Instagram . No cause of death was made immediately available. “Yesterday my father, Victor Miller, went to his final reward. He was almost always the smartest, funniest person in whatever room he was in. He inspired in me, and many others, a love of photography, music, and storytelling,” he wrote. “He had a helluva run and will be missed dearly.” Related Stories TV Richard O'Sullivan, British Sitcom Star Who Inspired John Ritter's 'Three's Company' Character, Dies at 82 Business Raffaele Annecchino, Former CEO of Paramount International, Dies at 55 Miller’s son added that a celebration of life will be held in November, “on Friday the 13th, of course.” He penned the script for Sean S. Cunningham’s beloved 1980 horror classic alongside Ron Kurz. The first film paved the way for a number of sequels, though Miller only served as the screenwriter for the original. He also worked with Cunningham again on 1982’s A Stranger Is Watching , and lent his talents to a myriad of television shows. Some of the TV projects Miller wrote for include One Life to Live , Another World, Guiding Light, General Hospital and All My Children . “Visionary screenwriter Victor Miller unequivocally etched his name in the classic horror film genre pantheon by penning the original script for the first Friday the 13 th film,” Professor Rel Dowdell, director of film studies at Hampton University, said in a statement shared with The Hollywood Reporter . “The screenplay, along with the film’s taut direction and production, launched one of the most famed and enduring franchises in history for over four decades.” Miller is survived by his wife, two sons and his grandson. title: ‘A Long Winter’ Review: Fred Hechinger and Ebon Moss-Bachrach Shine as Family Thrust Into Uneasy Isolation in Andrew Haigh’s Fine-Grained Drama
full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 7:30pm From left: Fred Hechinger and Ebon Moss-Bachrach in 'A Long Winter.' Mubi The many ways in which writer-director Andrew Haigh and fiction author Colm Tóibín share a kinship of sensibilities, notably in their impeccable gifts for intimate character observation, breathe warming embers into the sub-zero elemental severity of A Long Winter . A coming-of-age drama that touches delicately on grief and resilience, family and home, queer sexuality and liberating self-discovery, the film’s muted tone will be considered under-powered by some. But audiences willing to tune in to its slow-burn introspection and immersive sense of place will find a humanity that is its own reward, particularly in the probing performances of Fred Hechinger , Ebon Moss-Bachrach and D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai . Related Stories Movies 'Tender Loving Care' Review: Kate O'Flynn Lights Up Mike Leigh's Warm, Gently Wrenching Study of Solace and Solidarity Movies In Her New Movie, Carrie Coon Plays an Unexpected Cult Member: It's Easy to Say "No Way That Would Ever Happen to Me" Just as Haigh transposed the Japanese source novel from Tokyo to London in his 2023 stunner, All of Us Strangers , his adaptation of Tóibín’s novella — first published in the Irish author’s haunting 2006 short story collection Mothers and Sons before being issued as a standalone volume last year — relocates from the Spanish Pyrenees to Colorado’s Rocky Mountains. That landscape, magnificent but forbidding as fall lapses into the protracted, snowbound season that gives the film its title, helps make the material Haigh’s own, like a lost literary nugget of 1950s Americana. A Long Winter The Bottom Line Restrained but deeply felt. Venue : Telluride Film Festival Cast : Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitríona Balfe, Kit Connor, D’Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai, David Furr, Manuel Garcia-Rulfo, Martin Freeman, Geoff Gustafson, Anthony Timpano Director-screenwriter : Andrew Haigh, based on the novella by Colm Tóibín 1 hour 59 minutes The central character and the eyes and ears of the story is Mike (Hechinger), who took a test run at life on a farm two state lines away from his family’s cabin high in the mountains but was soon pulled back by homesickness. Mike is resistant to change, but for his younger brother Tommy ( Kit Connor ), it can’t come quickly enough. Impatient to see more of the world, he has enlisted in the Army and soon ships out to Korea, leaving the other bed empty in the room the brothers had shared since childhood. Change turns out to be beyond Mike’s control when he realizes that his depressed mother, Louise (Caitríona Balfe), is drinking heavily, increasingly chafing at the life of isolation her husband Lester (Moss-Bachrach) has chosen for them. Desperate for a connection to a more sophisticated world and its people, Louise entrusts Mikey to slip copies of Cosmopolitan among the provisions they pick up on trips to the fading foothills township. She knows Lester would disapprove of her spending what little money they have on frivolous pleasures. When Lester, whose father and grandfather both drank themselves to death, starts smelling booze on Louise’s breath again, he enrages her by tipping her secret stash of gut-rot wine down the sink. Unsettled to see his mother suffering, Mike urges his dad to give her what she needs, but Lester insists on her going cold-turkey, causing her to howl in anguish. While Lester and Mikey are out fixing the barn door before the season’s first big storm, Louise vanishes, taking her winter coat and boots with her. As the snow closes in and the phone lines and power go down, local residents and state troopers form a search party, trudging as far as they can go each day on the surrounding mountain range. Louise’s brother Jack ( Martin Freeman ), who lives on the other side of the mountain, has heard nothing from his sister. Family friend Joe (Manuel Garcia-Rulfo), who has started talking to prickly Lester again after a period of chilly silence, tells Mikey to look out for vultures circling overhead, usually a sure sign of a body in the snow. Haigh expertly balances the tone as dread turns to lacerating sorrow. But even as Mike faces the void of his mother’s absence in uncomfortable isolation with his disgruntled dad, his eyes can’t help locking with those of a young cop (Anthony Timpano) involved in the search, in what is instantly recognizable as unspoken sexual tension. While queer characters and themes run through the work of both Haigh and Tóibín, A Long Winter never takes the expected turns, although Mikey does have homoerotic fantasies about the cop in Tommy’s bed. Gay yearning is embedded in who he is, played with a touching cherubic innocence alongside a more adult longing by the reliably excellent Hechinger. When Mike insists on going out alone to continue the search each day, long after his dad has abandoned hope, the rigidly patriarchal Lester grumbles about there being no one to tend to the cooking and housework. When he hires mixed-race orphan Jimmy (Woon-A-Tai, one of the revelations of Reservation Dogs ) as a live-in domestic to handle those responsibilities, Mikey’s desire shifts focus. Whether or not it’s reciprocated is kept ambiguous by both Haigh and Woon-A-Tai. But after intially treating Jimmy dismissively and resenting the stranger’s presence in Tommy’s bed, Mike comes to his defense when Lester obnoxiously mocks the housekeeper one night for doing women’s work. While Jimmy can stand up for himself, the gesture of solidarity sparks a thaw between him and Mike. They start going out together each day to search, walking farther afield each time and pissing off Lester. Mikey’s gayness is very much a part of the character’s DNA, but it’s not the dominant thread of Haigh’s film. The writer-director is more attentive to the tectonic shifts in a family when the balance is upset, and the way that crushing loss can sometimes be a path to personal growth. Through his friendship with the quiet, soulful Jimmy, who has led a tough life, Mike gains the confidence to assert his place in the household, to deepen his sense of belonging in their lonely corner of the world, and to speak blunt truths to his father. The remote cabin he built was always Lester’s dream, never Louise’s. Even when Mike gains a deeper understanding of his mother and learns the reason that his father and their neighbor down the road, Ben (David Furr), detest each other, it appears that he will continue to hold his dad accountable. As always with Haigh, the entire ensemble is strong, led by Hechinger with raw pain, burgeoning maturity and innate sweetness. Moss-Bachrach deftly finds the softer sides of Lester, even at his most unreasonable, indicating that world-weary sadness eats away at him even if he has trouble showing it. Connor is appealing in the smallest role; Balfe leaves an indelible mark, giving Louise an addict’s cunning but also the gnawing frustration of a woman stuck in a life she didn’t want; and Woon-A-Tai brings a restorative calm — never at risk of becoming a noble old-school Sundance cliché. The film looks beautiful, its enveloping crystalline images gracefully shot on 35mm by DP André Turpin on location in the Canadian Rockies (cheaper than Colorado). Production designer Emmanuel Fréchette’s rustic, built-from-scratch cabin, complete with interiors and windows looking out onto the vast expanse of unforgiving nature, gives the movie a fully lived-in feel. And erstwhile Tangerine Dream member Paul Haslinger’s pensive score echoes the gentle rhythms of Jonathan Alberts’ editing. A Long Winter is not an emotional stealth bomb like All of Us Strangers or even Haigh’s 2011 breakthrough Weekend — it’s arguably closest in spirit to another of the Brit director’s American-set dramas, the under-appreciated but lovely Lean on Pete — but the new film’s subdued intensity and aching sensitivity make it lingeringly affecting.
