title: ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Kate O’Flynn Lights Up Mike Leigh’s Warm, Gently Wrenching Study of Solace and Solidarity
full_text: × Skip to main content By Jon Frosch Plus Icon Jon Frosch Senior Editor, Reviews jon_frosch Follow Sign Up View All September 4, 2026 6:47pm Kate O'Flynn (right) and Alice Bailey Johnson in 'Tender Loving Care.' Courtesy of Joseph Lynn/Thin Man Films Ltd/Bleecker Street A drama dotted with laughs (or a comedy blotted with pain?) in which everyday problems are confronted, and avoided, over steaming cuppas and brimming glasses of white wine, Tender Loving Care explores friendship, family dynamics and England’s fraying social safety net. In other words, it’s a Mike Leigh film, and a lovely one at that. If it ends up being his last, as the 83-year-old writer-director has indicated, it’s a fitting and stealthily powerful way to go out — a low-key mic drop of sorts. The movie is warm and inviting, filled with giggles and gossip and gentle gallows humor; it’s also wrenching, with a topical urgency simmering just beneath the jovial surface. While Leigh’s left-wing politics inform the story, the filmmaker, unlike his contemporary Ken Loach, mostly avoids playing ventriloquist; the chit-chatting, chortling, sobbing, seething souls who populate his work tend to be too complicated, too insistently human to serve as mere spokespeople for their creator’s ideas. Related Stories Movies In Her New Movie, Carrie Coon Plays an Unexpected Cult Member: It's Easy to Say "No Way That Would Ever Happen to Me" Movies Telluride Film Fest Kicks Off with Brunch, 'Wild Horse Nine' North American Premiere Tender Loving Care The Bottom Line A lovely addition — and likely conclusion — to an exceptional career. Venue: Telluride Film Festival Cast: Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson, Kate O’Flynn, Alice Bailey Johnson Director-screenwriter: Mike Leigh 1 hour 47 minutes In Tender Loving Care , those ideas concern compassion, solidarity and support — what it means to look out for one another at this (angry, angering) point in history, specifically in a country whose public services have been eroded by an ethos of self-reliance codified by Thatcher and further cemented, or perverted, by Brexit. As is often the case in Leigh’s films, the thematic framework is conspicuous; characters, on occasion, turn subtext into text, delivering mini-disquisitions on the failures of the state and the isolation of urban life today. Those statements might register as distractingly didactic if they didn’t sound wholly believable coming out of these particular people’s mouths; two of the four central figures, childhood BFFs Amy ( Kate O’Flynn , Widow’s Bay scene-stealer) and Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson), are overextended, underappreciated social workers — and seasoned compartmentalizers, lest the despondency they witness daily on the job pull them under. Amy and Rosie, as well as Amy’s kindly parents Birdie (Marion Bailey, Leigh’s longtime partner) and Geoff (Paul Jesson), arrive onscreen fully formed, alive with personal and relational histories we can intuit beyond what’s in the frame. If it feels like we’ve known these folks forever — from Amy and Rosie’s mutual hype sessions to Birdie and Geoff’s puttering and banter — that’s a credit to Leigh’s legendary rehearsal process, during which he and his actors build the characters from scratch through weeks of improvisation and discussion. Nothing and everything happens over the course of Tender Loving Care . Unceremoniously dumped by a boyfriend who’s gone back to his wife and child, Amy moves in with single-and-mingling Rosie. Birdie frets about Amy’s romantic and reproductive prospects, though she and Geoff console themselves with their certainty that she’s better off sans her ex. Amy and Rosie endure stressful days on the job (Amy works mainly with children, Rosie with the elderly), retreating to their flat in the evenings to swap horror stories or decompress over girl talk, dance-offs and other bursts of booze-infused silliness. Geoff’s health takes a sudden turn for the worse. The tone here is mellower, the pitch less heightened than in Leigh’s more volatile domestic tragicomedies, like Secrets & Lies and Life Is Sweet , to say nothing of the bludgeoning All or Nothing . That’s in large part a reflection of the new film’s main quartet, who sit at the opposite end of the temperamental spectrum from Pansy, the ferocious protagonist of Leigh’s previous effort, 2024’s Hard Truths . Amy, Rosie, Birdie and Geoff are indeed among the most amiable characters Leigh has ever created, their darker feelings — loneliness, jealousy, rage, dread — tucked safely beneath chipper smiles and cheerful pleasantries. But Leigh has never been one to flinch at life’s cruelties. The simplicity of Tender Loving Care ’s narrative, the sweetness of the people it portrays, and the ticklish good vibes they generate belie a toughmindedness about both the private disappointments and the larger societal injustices that shake our respective worlds. When moments of anguish arrive — a neighbor’s tormented account of her husband’s funeral; a tirade by a paranoia-gripped hoarder Rosie is assigned to visit; a hard-drinking mother’s fury at the foster care system for which Amy is assessing her — they have a rawness and force that slice right through the movie’s congeniality. The film is in direct conversation with Hard Truths , as well as Leigh standouts Another Year and Happy-Go-Lucky , in its consideration of what determines happiness — the degrees to which choice, disposition, luck and broader structural or socioeconomic forces play a part. Like so much of Leigh’s work, Tender Loving Care ponders how people of different circumstances and constitutions coexist: how we make each other feel and act, how our perception of each other’s lives shapes our perception of our own. It’s also about how we proceed with the business of living amid hardships both mundane and momentous. Like Ozu , a clear influence, Leigh is one of the medium’s great observers of human behavior, from the small talk that drowns out the terror of our worst anxieties to the self-delusions that sustain us during our most vulnerable moments to the way we accept or refuse help — the latter sometimes misguidedly. “I can’t put it on them,” Amy tells Rosie, explaining her reluctance to let her parents know of her break-up. Like all the film’s principals, Amy is an expert practitioner of Britain’s famed stiff upper lip, but here she’s sparing Birdie and Geoff a burden they’re more than ready to share. O’Flynn is an expressive marvel, her kooky lightheartedness periodically clouding over with a melancholy that cuts to the bone. The swirl of conflicting emotions that play out across Amy’s face as she gulps champagne while listening to her mother reminisce about her courtship with Geoff is astonishing — a piercing pantomime of the oft-cited notion that millennials are the first generation to have fewer opportunities than their parents. Bailey Johnson, a casual charisma bomb, makes Rosie so radiant and grounded and fun that you may realize only late in the film — when she reveals she no longer speaks to her own mom and dad — that her generosity toward the other characters is more symbiotic than selfless. Rosie is the very definition of a ride-or-die, but she needs Amy and her family as much as they need her. The beautifully synced Bailey and Jesson, meanwhile, offer a duet of endearments, confidences, worries and innocuous shit-talk, conjuring the ineffable mix of intimacy and distance that makes a long-term marriage. When the rhythm of their relationship is disrupted in the film’s second half, the effect is devastating. Visually, Tender Loving Care is characterized by Leigh’s typical unfussiness, with Lucy Bristow taking over DP duties from frequent Leigh collaborator Dick Pope, who died in 2024 . As usual, there’s mastery in how the filmmaker uses facial close-ups to add notes of tension, encouraging the viewer to locate truths undisclosed by the dialogue. Ditto in how he deploys a single overhead shot — serene but conspicuous — to foreshadow an unlucky swerve in the story. A touching penultimate scene feels like a natural conclusion to this portrait of people devotedly closing ranks when crisis strikes. But Leigh doesn’t stop there, instead punctuating his film with a final image of uncommon bluntness and despair. At first impression, it seems an incongruously — if not unjustifiably — hopeless way to go out. Yet given the dogged humanism that is the throughline of Leigh’s extraordinary filmography, perhaps a less pessimistic reading is due: Leigh is ending his movie, possibly his career, with a plea for individuals to lift up those they know and love, of course, but also to fight for a society that lifts up those they don’t. title: ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Kate O’Flynn Stars In What Could Be Mike Leigh’s Final Film, But It Happens To Be One Of His Best – Telluride Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Kate O’Flynn Stars In What Could Be Mike Leigh’s Final Film, But It Happens To Be One Of His Best – Telluride Film Festival View All September 4, 2026 6:47pm ‘Tender Loving Care' Thin Man Films There has been much talk in film circles that the great Mike Leigh ‘s latest film, Tender Loving Care , might be his last. Health issues, general aging and other things can get in the way for all of us, but if this turns out to be his finale, at least in terms of feature films — he has made 22, and another 20 stage plays — it is nice to report that this warm film, which, combined with 2024’s Hard Knocks, returns the seven-time Oscar nominee to the honest stories of British family life he has done so well in his remarkable career. This one, however, finds the director in a mood to confront the inevitable changes and march of time, its joys and sadness in the lives of ordinary people going about living it. Tender Loving Care had its world premiere Friday at the Telluride Film Festival. Related Stories Festivals Telluride Film Festival Lineup: ‘Elsinore’ With Andrew Scott And Olivia Colman; Jesse Eisenberg’s ‘The Debut’; Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ And More Set For World Premieres Reviews Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Leigh famously makes films in a very different manner than most, pulling together his cast and then workshopping them with an outline of where the scenario might head, but with no script. He spends up to six months with them — shaping, exploring and developing the characters that later will become the core of the screenplay Leigh writes. He has put together a troupe of actors over the decades since his first film in the early ’70s, and a lot of them return again and again. And many have for Tender Loving Care , including frequent collaborators Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson, along with Bailey’s real-life daughter, Alice Bailey Johnson, who also appeared in two more recent Leigh productions. New to the process and Leigh’s world is current Widow’s Bay Emmy favorite Kate O’Flynn who, no surprise, fits right in. Watch on Deadline

title: Kenneth Branagh Hosts Judi Dench, Anthony Hopkins, Ian McKellen, Gary Oldman & Helen Mirren In Telluride-Bound Doc ‘Into The Breach’
full_text: Skip to main content By Baz Bamigboye Baz Bamigboye Columnist/International Editor At Large @BazBam More Stories By Baz Baz Bamigboye Looks Back On True Tabloid Life With ‘Ink’ Director Danny Boyle & Writer James Graham – Venice Film Festival Breaking Baz: Broadway’s Intoxicating ‘Buena Vista Social Club’ Musical Eyes London Transfer In 2027, Say Producers Orin Wolf & Barbara Broccoli Breaking Baz: ‘MobLand’s Joanne Froggatt In Advanced Talks To Play Quaker Leader In MGM+’s ‘The Magnificent Seven’ Remake View All September 4, 2026 6:28pm From left: Anthony Hopkins, Freddie Fox and Judi Dench shoot ’Into the Breach’ Jenni Carvell Judi Dench tells firsthand how stage stars such as Richard Burton, John Neville and later Anthony Hopkins , were the rock stars of the theater in the postwar years in the UK. The likes of Burton and Neville, in particular, were treated like gods. “That was before the Beatles,” Dame Judi remarks in Into the Breach , the enthralling documentary co-created by Freddie Fox with Richard Fullerton and produced by Kenneth Branagh and his Kenneth Branagh Company. The movie has its world premiere screenings at the Telluride Film Festival beginning Sunday with showings at the Sheridan Opera House and the Backlot. Related Stories Festivals Telluride Film Festival Lineup: ‘Elsinore’ With Andrew Scott And Olivia Colman; Jesse Eisenberg’s ‘The Debut’; Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ And More Set For World Premieres Reviews Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews It was, as Dame Judi puts it, a “pre-Beatles fever that the two of them [Burton and Neville] created at the Vic.” Watch on Deadline For her part, she got to perform opposite John Gielgud and Peggy Ashcroft in The Cherry Orchard , which led to her being cast as Juliet in director Franco Zeffirelli’s 1960 Old Vic production of Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet . Dench says winning the role was all down to Gielgud choosing her for The Cherry Orchard . “It was like putting a stake in a wilting plant,” Dame Judi says during a moment in Into the Breach , adding that she was the plant while Gielgud was the stake. Forever after, she was “at his feet.” That idolatry also was down to the fact that Gielgud “obeyed the verse and lines, and he did everything that I believe should be done in Shakespeare.” Hopkins, another member of the Old Vic company, says in the film that he was lucky to have acted alongside Gielgud and Laurence Olivier on stage. Hopkins and Gielgud also appeared in David Lynch’s The Elephant Man starring John Hurt. Impishly, Hopkins recalls that Gielgud was growing weary after doing “take after take” of one scene. “Sir John said, ‘”’When do we finish? I haven’t got long to live.’” However, Into the Breach does speak of the theater’s importance to cinema. After all, Hopkins was cast as Hannibal Lector in The Silence of the Lambs after director Jonathan Demme saw him in landmark play Pravda at the National Theatre in 1985. In Pravda , Hopkins plays a reptilian-like newspaper magnate modeled by playwrights David Hare and Howard Brenton on Rupert Murdoch. (Go see Danny Boyle’s searing movie Ink , based on James Graham’s stage play, which is also playing up in the Colorado mountains this weekend.)

full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond , Damon Wise September 4, 2026 1:20pm Clockwise from top left: 'Primetime,' 'Ink,' 'Bunker,' 'The Echo Chamber' and 'Bucking Fastard' A24; Anthony Dickenson; Blue Morning Pictures; Indigo Film; Lena Herzog The 2026 Venice Film Festival got underway on Wednesday, September 2, with Oscar-winning English director Danny Boyle’s Ink — starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy — kicking off an 83rd edition that includes films starring the likes of Robert Pattinson, Penelope Cruz & Javier Bardem, Jack Huston & Sofia Boutella, Dakota Johnson, John Malkovich & Sam Rockwell, Alicia Vikander & Susan Sarandon, Nick Nolte and Kate & Rooney Mara in their first movie together. Related Stories Festivals Venice Film Festival 2026 Photos: Opening Ceremony, ‘Ink’ Premiere & George Clooney Lifetime Achievement Presentation Festivals Venice Head Talks Studio Absence, Dearth Of Female Golden Lion Contenders & Why Neon Nixed Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’ – Q&A Along with Ink, this year’s competition lineup includes such buzzy titles seeking awards-season glory as Florian Zeller’s Bunker, Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime , Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love , Andrea Pallaoro’s The Echo Chamber , Casey Affleck’s Company and Warner Herzog’s Bucking Fastard. Studio titles largely are absent this year, but the overall lineup also includes new films by Luca Guadagnino, Paul Schrader and Wim Wenders along with Laura Poitras’ short about ICE protests in Minnesota, and Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace’s doc on the comeback of rock band Oasis. Watch on Deadline Check out Deadline’s reviews out of Venice, and keep checking back as we add more. Click on each headline to read our full review. The Basics of Philosophy ‘The Basics of Philosophy’ Noora Films Section: Out of Competition Director: Paul Schrader Cast: Jack Huston, Sofia Boutella, Daniel Zovalto, Bill Pullman, Dana Delany, Shiloh Fernandez, Karl Glusman, Elizabeth Petruso, Santiago Cabrera, Trevor Dolden, Richard Gere Deadline’s takeaway: With this introspective character study, Schrader continues to making the kind of grownup films we rarely get to see anymore, outside of Europe at least. He never presents easy answers in his movies — same with this deep dive into the philosophy of life and the key question we can ask of many Schrader characters, “Can we change?” — PH Bucking Fastard ‘Bucking Fastard’ Lena Herzog Section: Competition Director-screenwriter: Werner Herzog Cast: Kate Mara, Rooney Mara, Orlando Bloom, Domhnall Gleeson Deadline’s takeaway: Although it appears to start with a tone of gentle mockery, there’s something quite sweet and generous at work beneath the stylized strangeness of the tale of two sisters played by Rooney and Kate Mara, a tone that Werner Herzog has never really struck before in his fiction work, with the possible exception of 2019’s Family Romance LLC . — DW The Girl with the Leica ‘The Girl with the Leica’ Manuel Alberto Claro Section: Orizzonti Director: Alina Marazzi Cast: Emilia Schüle, Aaron Altaras, Luna Wedler, Lucas Englander, Thomas Schubert, Sebastian Schneider, Idan Weiss, Lia von Blarer, Hans-Christian Hegewald, Jeremy Mockridge, Joel Basman Deadline’s takeaway: The jazzed-up, unconventional biopic of the late photojournalist Gerda Taro asks questions about the the fine line between bravery and ego in the process of bringing back dispatches from the front line, but its structure over-complicates a simple yet quite profound meditation on an artist’s identity and legacy. — DW Ink ‘Ink’ Netflix Section: Competition Director: Danny Boyle Cast: Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce, Claire Foy, Jonathan Hyde, Lucy Russell, Abigail Amin, Bertie Carvel, Brian Gleeson, Christopher Fulford, Patrick Kennedy, Blake Harrison, Georgie Henley Deadline’s takeaway: Danny Boyle with his whip-smart, in-your-face stye is the perfect filmmaker to bring this world set in 1969 London to life as the brash if trash visionary Rupert Murdoch and his hand-picked editor-in-chief launch what would become a new era of tabloid journalism, changing the media world for better or worse in the process. Here all the cylinders are firing, and it is thrilling stuff indeed. — PH Wild Horse Nine ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Searchlight Pictures Section: Competition Director: Martin McDonagh Cast: John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, Mariana di Girolamo, Ailín Salas, Tom Waits, Parker Posey Deadline’s takeaway: John Malkovich gives a career performance in a perfect if unexpected casting. This so-called “buddy movie” of a wildly different stripe easily is one of the year’s best films, and in its own peculiar way the most spiritual. Continuing a trend among film festivals this year, the 53rd Telluride Film Festival, which kicks off Friday and runs through Labor Day, will apparently not be featuring any big major studio releases, and instead is revealing a heavily stacked indie lineup of world premieres, North American debuts, and at least eight films first seen on the Croisette in May. The closest we are getting to studio output this year will be one movie each from Telluride regulars Focus Features and Searchlight, the specialty divisions respectively of Universal and Disney which will be on hand to launch domestic awards season campaigns for their hopefuls. Olivia Colman co-stars. Watch on Deadline
